courseTitle: ChatGPT & Generative AI - The Complete Guide

cues.en: The last task here
was to get the AI to write an
email or a draft for an email, which you
wanna send to a colleague, where you wanna tell that
colleague that you need feedback on your submitted
prototype until the end of the week.
And here's one example prompt
I came up with. Unlike in the
other prompts, I did not add a role here
because it didn't seem suitable to me for this
specific task. You could, of course, do it though.
Instead, here, I have my
instruction but I then also provide
some hopefully helpful pieces of context.
For example, I describe what the email should be
about... (pauses) and I add the
piece of context that I need that
reply until the end of the week.
I also, and that's maybe the most important
part, describe the
tone of that email or how
it should be written by the
AI. I make it clear that it, of course, should be
polite, but that it's urgent
and that I need the feedback ASAP, as
soon as possible. So
that should be a very important, uh,
piece of context added to the prompt here,
hopefully increasing the chances of getting a
helpful response by the AI.
And if I sent this to ChatGPT,
still here in my case, I'm
getting this draft here,
even a suggestion for the subject, and
I would say that's a rather good draft.
I can probably use this as is and just
fill in the blanks, and that's, by the way, something you should always
do. Always read that output. We've all
gotten those AI-generated emails where people
forgot to fill in the blanks, and that is quite
embarrassing. So always read it,
always refine it, always fill in the blanks, but
I think the AI wrote a pretty good
email draft here also thanks to
our prompt, of course.
Another prompting technique that can
sometimes be very useful is
self-reflective prompting. And what does
this mean? It means that you might
already have a response
generated by the AI, like this
example response here, but it doesn't matter.
Could be a response to any kind of problem, any kind of
output you have by the AI.
And of course, as you learned before, it's a chat.
You can refine it. You can tell the AI to, for example,
remove emojis from here. You can do all that, and you
might wanna do all that. But you
can also ask the
AI to
self-analyze its output and
come up with improvements. For example, you
could tell it to analyze its output. What's
good about it, what's bad, and how could it be improved?
And this is, of course, now also in the
context window. This output is in there just as
your original prompt is still in there because
it's always the entire chat history that's in the
context window? And therefore, you'll now get a new
output that might be even better than the original
output, or you might get a summary of
things that could be improved, like this here,
where it's analyzing the output and
it then tells you what
seems to be good and what might
be improved, or what could be improved.
And then in my case here, it even gives me a revised
version. If it didn't provide that
version, we could, of course, simply tell it
to use its analysis
here to write a new version of the post.
But here, it's already doing that for me.
And this self-reflective prompting,
combined with your instructions and your
feedback, can therefore be
a great way of improving
results generated by the AI.
You can also be more direct than I
was here in my follow-up prompt.
I asked it to analyze it and
asked it to answer what's good, what's bad,
and so on. You could, of course, also do something
like sending a follow-up message like this.
After all, it's not a human, so I guess you don't have
to care for any feelings.
And that, of course, also will get the AI to
complete the sequence and then
give you a revised version of the post or give
you an analysis of what could be, uh, a
problem with the original post based on
your criticism here.
Now, this is something you naturally
already might have done in the past. We all
had responses that did not hit the
mark at all. But it's important to be
aware of this self-reflective prompting
technique, especially also when you're getting a
response that is quite good but that
maybe can still be improved a bit more.
So even if you're happy with the output
generated by an AI, asking it
to analyze it and potentially improve it
can be a good idea.
Another important prompting technique
is so-called negative prompting.
For example, if you have a prompt like this, where you
want ChatGPT, in this case, to create a
list of advantages of using generative AI
over search engines like Google, you
might have certain aspects,
certain possible advantages it might list
that should not be included in the response.
You might, in general, no matter which kind of prompt you are
sending to the AI, have certain
aspects you don't want to have
considered by the AI for its
response. For example here, I might not
be interested in the advantage of
ads missing in generative AI
output. Of course, that is an advantage compared to
Google, for example, that we don't have to scroll
through a bunch of ads, but it might not be what I'm
looking for here. So therefore, in that case, I
could add this extra piece of context to my
prompt, "Don't cover any
ads-related advantages," making
it clear that for this list of advantages,
ad-related stuff should not be part of that
list. And that's negative prompting
because I'm not asking for something.
Instead, I'm asking for something to
not be considered or included.
And again, like with all these techniques, this is not a technique
you have to use exclusively or all the
time. Instead, it can simply be a technique that
makes sense for some prompts and that can, of
course, also be combined with other techniques
like chain-of-thought prompting or any
other prompt engineering technique.
So here, in this case, this will hopefully give me a list of
advantages and hopefully, none of those
advantages has anything to do with
ads. And that is indeed
looking quite good to me here.
So at this point, we had a look at many techniques
that can hopefully all lead to better
output. But pretty much all of these
techniques focused on the output
content, to have more
meaningful, helpful content be generated.
Another important aspect of AI
output, however, is the format of that
output. And thus far, we pretty
much exclusively dealt with plain text,
maybe with the exception of this one translation
example where I asked for a list of
translated words. And indeed, that
already was a useful example for also
understanding that you cannot just
control the content, but also the
format of the output. You
can ask for lists, for
lists that have a certain format like in that
translation task, but you can also ask
for other kinds of structuring or
formatting. For example, I might wanna
use an AI model like ChatGPT here
to generate some dummy sales data. And I'm telling the
AI which kind of information, which kind of
data should be included in every data point.
Now especially for tasks like this, but
also in general, whenever I maybe wanna use
that output in some other
software or some other
process, I might need the data in a
specific format. For example, here I'm
not just asking for a specific number of entries, but
most importantly, I'm defining some rules
for the format of the output. Of course, it will
still be text technically, but the text
should be formatted in a certain way.
Specifically here, I want the output
to use the CSV format. And I
just want the data, no other text,
no extra explanations.
Now a prompt like this or an extra
instruction like this is no guarantee
for ChatGPT or any other AI
model to really follow your
instructions. It might still give you some extra
text. It might have errors in the output
format. But it increases the
likelihood that you get an output
in the requested format. So for example here,
that it indeed gives me only this
CSV formatted text and
nothing else, which of course means that I could
now just grab that, paste it into some text
file, save it as a CSV, and use that
in my simulations, data
analysis exercises, or wherever I
want to use it. And of course, we're
not limited to CSV. I
could also ask for markdown. For example
here, where I want the AI to generate a blog
post which I then wanna use in my
own markdown parsing pipeline. So
I don't wanna have the plain text, I wanna have the
unparsed markdown.
And of course, here typically I would add more context, more
information, but this example of course is about
the output formatting, not about the actual
content. Of course, typically you wanna optimize
both content and formatting if a
specific formatting is needed. But this
shows us that we, for example, can then also
get the unparsed markdown,
which I could now copy and paste into my
blog engine that might require
markdown input, for example. And
you can of course request any kind of output
in any shape you need. For example here,
I want plain text, I don't want
CSV or markdown or JSON, but I
want that text to have a certain
inherent structure. And
indeed here we could also combine this with
few-shot prompting to give one or two
examples. But here I'll
first try without any specific examples
and just define my output
format, the structure of the output I wanna have.
And that then hopefully is enough
to have a list be generated that
follows this structure where I have
some title and then a short explanation.
And indeed it looks like that's the case here for
me. And that's
there for another important part of prompting, that you
cannot just control the
content, but also the format
of that content for your output.

lectures.title: Let The AI Help You With Prompting!

cues.en: Last but not least, here's
another trick many people
actually don't think about (laughs) , even though it's obvious once
you know it. You're dealing with a
generative AI model, right?
It generates text, so you can,
of course, also have it generate
prompts for you. And it
won't be great at that because
that's what it needs as an input. It doesn't have
any knowledge about that. It's just generating
text and completing sequences, after all,
but it is, of course, simply another piece
of content that can be generated by AI
models, just like they can generate blog
posts. They can also generate
prompts for you. And of course,
modern models have a general
understanding of what a prompt
is because their training data
of recent models includes
articles about prompt engineering from the
first wave of AI models. So
there is some knowledge about prompting in the training
data already nowadays, and
that's why you can, of course, ask ChatGPT
or any other model to generate a
prompt for a given problem for you.
And as always, you don't just have to use that
prompt then. You shouldn't blindly trust it or
just copy and paste it, though you can, of course,
do that if you're happy with it. But you can use it as a
starting point to maybe combine it with
your own knowledge about prompting and your own thoughts
about what should go into such a prompt.
But asking ChatGPT or any other
AI model for tips regarding
defining a prompt and how good prompts would look like
is, of course, definitely something you might wanna
do to use all the knowledge you
gained throughout this model with all the knowledge
(laughs) the internet, and therefore, the AI model has
to write the best possible prompts.
So in this section, you learned a
lot about prompt engineering, a lot of important
techniques that will apply no matter which
provider you're using, no matter with which
AI model you're interacting. I
also wanna mention though that some
of these providers like Anthropic,
but for example, also OpenAI
published their own prompt engineering
guides. And you can and should of course, also
visit those guides if you are
interacting with models by those companies because
who would know better than the creators of these
models on how to efficiently use them or
work with them? Now in those prompt
engineering guides, you'll find many
explanations that you also saw in
this section here, many techniques that you also
saw in this section here. But still,
it's worth going through these guides to learn a bit
more or to learn about
model-specific tricks that might get you better
results when working with Anthropic models
than when working with ChatGPT, for
example. And that's there for just
another side note that besides the general,
very powerful and important techniques you learned about
in this section, you also might wanna
visit those guides that were published by
those AI companies.
This section gave you a
thorough overview of important
prompt engineering techniques, tips and tricks,
and recommendations. Now, of course,
in the end, prompt engineering is just
about sending some text to an AI
in order to get back some text, and therefore,
anything that works for you and th- that gets a job done
is a good solution. You should
not overthink prompt
engineering. You should just be aware of
these different techniques. Consider combining
some of these techniques simply depending on
what you're trying to achieve, and
especially if you're using an AI and you're not
happy with the results you're getting, you might wanna
revisit this section and revisit certain techniques
and simply experiment with those techniques and
with variations of prompts to
ultimately get results that get the
job done for you.
